blocks.content: Misreading a simple 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' in a question stem is the single most common cause of negative marks.

rows: Hiding 'NOT' or 'INCORRECT' in a long stem
Providing data in mixed units (e.g., meters & km)
Standardize units in the first line of working
Putting a partial truth as Option A
Mandatorily read all options from A to D
Inserting tedious steps solvable by estimation
Use digit sum, unit digit, or estimation

items: Examiners design 'distractor' options that match common calculation errors made mid-way through a problem.
Questions asking for 'INCORRECT' statements often trick students into marking a correct statement instead.
Do not assume 'All of the above' is correct without validating at least two options independently.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Always highlight critical qualifier words like 'NOT', 'EXCEPT', 'ALWAYS', and 'INCORRECT' in the question prompt.
Beware of Option A bias, where examiners place a plausible but wrong answer early to trap hasty candidates.
Double-check unit conversions (e.g., converting km/h to m/s or minutes to seconds) before finalizing numerical answers.
Avoid spending excess time on high-difficulty questions early in the paper; prioritize quick wins first.
Use the process of elimination to systematically eliminate improbable options before making an educated guess.
